body:
# Scale and Convergence: Replicating 'Bigger Models Correlate More' Within One Family

**Problem:** Correlated Errors found larger, more accurate models have more correlated errors, even across providers — suggesting capability drives convergence. This was shown across heterogeneous models; a controlled within-family size sweep would isolate scale as the driver.

**Direction:** Replicate the error-correlation-vs-accuracy relationship using a single open family released at multiple sizes (e.g. Qwen2.5 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B/14B, or Llama-3.2 1B/3B + Llama-3-8B). Measure pairwise error correlation on a benchmark as a function of size, testing whether bigger pairs converge more. Twist: also compare cross-family same-size pairs to separate 'scale' from 'shared lineage'.

**Why it matters:** If convergence is an intrinsic consequence of scaling, then homogeneity (and correlated failure) will *worsen* as the field advances — a long-horizon systemic-risk trajectory worth documenting cheaply. Pure inference on open checkpoints.

**Relevant context:** Controlled replication of the scale-correlation finding in Correlated Errors in LLMs (arXiv:2506.07962) using a single open model family's size ladder.

# Distillation Lineage and Homogeneity: Do Children of the Same Teacher Cluster?

**Problem:** Many open models are distilled from a few teachers (GPT-4 outputs, R1). The Hivemind effect may be partly explained by *shared training-data lineage* rather than independent convergence. This causal angle is unmeasured.

**Direction:** Replicate inter-model homogeneity measurement but group models by known/declared lineage (e.g. R1-distilled vs. GPT-distilled vs. independently RLHF'd). Test whether same-lineage models are significantly more homogeneous than cross-lineage pairs on open-ended prompts. Twist: use clustering/dendrograms on output-similarity to see if the model 'family tree' recovers training lineage.

**Why it matters:** Identifying lineage as a driver of correlated failure tells deployers a concrete diversification rule (avoid same-teacher models), a directly actionable, lab-independent contribution to concentration-risk mitigation.

**Relevant context:** Extends Artificial Hivemind (arXiv:2510.22954) and the distillation-transfer literature; uses open models with documented lineages. Output-similarity clustering only.

# Replicating Hivemind on Moral/Value Judgments: Shared Ethical Blind Spots

**Problem:** Open-ended moral dilemmas are a domain where homogeneity is especially concerning: if all models give the same ethical verdict, society loses pluralism and inherits one model's value blind spots. Artificial Hivemind didn't isolate value-laden prompts.

**Direction:** Replicate the homogeneity analysis on a curated set of moral/value-laden open-ended questions (trolley-style, contested policy stances, cultural dilemmas). Measure inter-model agreement and stance-similarity across 8-10 open models. Twist: compare to the spread of *human* opinion (from existing survey data or Infinity-Chat annotations) to quantify how much narrower the model consensus is than human disagreement.

**Why it matters:** Homogeneous value judgments concentrate moral authority in a few models — a diffuse, long-horizon societal risk frontier labs are poorly positioned to study neutrally. Pure inference, public prompts, high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Value-domain replication of Artificial Hivemind (arXiv:2510.22954); can reuse Infinity-Chat's human-annotation spread as a human-diversity baseline.

# Temperature Doesn't Fix It: Replicating Persistent Collapse Across Sampling Settings

**Problem:** Diversity-collapse work claims collapse persists even at high temperature. This is a crucial, counterintuitive result for anyone hoping sampling tricks restore diversity, but it is often asserted on limited models. A systematic open-model sweep would confirm or bound it.

**Direction:** Replicate the 'high temperature doesn't recover diversity' claim across 4-5 open models and a temperature/top-p grid, measuring within-model diversity (distinct-n, embedding spread) and inter-model homogeneity at each setting. Twist: contrast naive temperature scaling against verbalized sampling and few-shot diversity prompts to chart which knobs actually move homogeneity.

**Why it matters:** Establishes which cheap, inference-time interventions genuinely reduce systemic homogeneity vs. merely adding noise — practical guidance for safety-conscious deployers, produced entirely outside a lab.

**Relevant context:** Replicates persistence-of-collapse claims ('Price of Format' arXiv:2505.18949; Verbalized Sampling arXiv:2510.01171) across open models and sampling settings.

# Hivemind Over Time: Are Newer Open Models More Homogeneous Than Older Ones?

**Problem:** If alignment pressure and shared data are driving convergence, homogeneity should be *increasing* over model generations. No replication tracks the Hivemind effect longitudinally across release dates.

**Direction:** Replicate inter-model homogeneity measurement on a chronologically ordered set of open instruct models (e.g. Llama-2-7B-chat, Mistral-7B-instruct-v0.1, Llama-3-8B-instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-instruct, Gemma-2-9B). Plot average pairwise output-similarity against release date on fixed open-ended prompts. Twist: separate same-era cross-family similarity to see whether convergence is accelerating field-wide.

**Why it matters:** A rising-homogeneity trend line is a compelling, simple visualization of a worsening systemic risk — exactly the long-horizon framing labs deprioritize. Pure inference on freely available historical checkpoints.

**Relevant context:** Longitudinal replication of Artificial Hivemind (arXiv:2510.22954) across model release generations; all checkpoints open on HuggingFace.

# Quantizing Doesn't Save You: Does Quantization Change a Model's Hivemind Position?

**Problem:** Deployers often run quantized open models. It is unknown whether quantization shifts a model's outputs enough to de-correlate it from the full-precision herd, or whether quantized variants remain in the same homogeneity cluster (offering no diversification benefit).

**Direction:** Replicate the homogeneity-clustering measurement comparing full-precision and several quantized versions (8-bit, 4-bit/GPTQ/AWQ) of the same open models on open-ended prompts. Twist: test whether quantization moves a model meaningfully in output-similarity space or whether quantized copies stay tightly clustered with their FP16 parent — i.e., is 'run a quantized variant' a real diversification lever?

**Why it matters:** Practical deployment guidance: if quantized variants don't break correlation, ensembling FP16+quantized gives false robustness. A cheap, concrete contribution to concentration-risk mitigation, runnable on one consumer GPU (quantization is the point).

**Relevant context:** Novel deployment-variant twist on Artificial Hivemind homogeneity measurement (arXiv:2510.22954); uses standard open quantization tooling (bitsandbytes/GPTQ).

# System-Prompt Persona Diversity: Can Personas Break the Hivemind?

**Problem:** A cheap proposed mitigation for homogeneity is assigning models different personas/system prompts. Whether persona-conditioning actually de-correlates a herd of models (rather than just restyling identical content) is untested at the inter-model level.

**Direction:** Replicate homogeneity measurement on a set of open models, then add the twist: condition each model with a varied system-prompt persona and re-measure inter-model output-similarity. Test whether personas reduce semantic (not just surface) convergence on open-ended and reasoning prompts. Use embedding similarity to separate stylistic from substantive diversity.

**Why it matters:** If personas only change style while substance stays homogeneous, a popular 'diversity by prompting' strategy is illusory for safety. A clean replication + intervention study with strong, lab-independent practical value.

**Relevant context:** Intervention twist on Artificial Hivemind homogeneity measurement (arXiv:2510.22954); prompt-only, open models.

# Replicating the Typicality-Bias Story: Do Models Converge on the 'Most Typical' Answer?

**Problem:** Verbalized Sampling traces mode collapse to a typicality bias in preference data (annotators favor familiar text). A testable prediction: when models converge, they converge specifically toward the most *typical/familiar* response, not a random one. This causal prediction hasn't been directly replicated as a homogeneity diagnostic.

**Direction:** Replicate by: for open-ended prompts, collect outputs from many open models, then measure whether the consensus output corresponds to the highest-typicality option (operationalized via base-model likelihood or human-rated familiarity from Infinity-Chat). Twist: show that models cluster around the typical answer and that VS shifts them toward rarer-but-valid answers, linking the mechanism to observed homogeneity.

**Why it matters:** Confirming typicality as the convergence axis gives a principled diversity intervention (penalize typicality) and explains *why* blind spots are shared. A mechanistic-flavored but fully inference-based study with high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Replicates the typicality-bias mechanism from Verbalized Sampling (arXiv:2510.01171), using Infinity-Chat familiarity annotations (arXiv:2510.22954) as the typicality signal.

# Hivemind in Hazard Identification: Do Models Share the Same Risk Blind Spots?

**Problem:** A safety-critical use of LLMs is flagging risks (in plans, code, instructions). If many models fail to flag the *same* hazards, layered LLM safety review is far weaker than it appears. The Hivemind method hasn't been applied to hazard-detection coverage.

**Direction:** Replicate homogeneity analysis on a hazard-identification task: give 8-10 open models a set of plans/instructions containing planted hazards (e.g. unsafe lab steps, risky financial advice) and record which hazards each model flags. Twist: compute the 'shared miss rate' — hazards missed by ALL models — and compare to what independent detectors would predict, directly quantifying correlated safety blind spots.

**Why it matters:** Layered LLM oversight is a core safety strategy; demonstrating correlated misses quantifies how much defense-in-depth homogeneity erodes. This is a model-organism-flavored evaluation of a fuzzy-reward task, ideal for lab-independent work.

**Relevant context:** Applies Artificial Hivemind's shared-blind-spot framing (arXiv:2510.22954) to a hazard-detection evaluation; open models, hand-built planted-hazard set.

# Decomposing 'measure honesty' into a calibration-vs-confidence probe slice

**Problem:** Honesty research asks what it means for a model to be honest. A measurable sub-problem from interpretability: does a model's internally-decodable confidence (probe) match its verbalized confidence, and when it states high confidence while internally uncertain, is that a detectable honesty failure?

**Direction:** Decompose 'measure honesty' into an internal-vs-stated confidence comparison. On a small open model over a QA set, train a probe to estimate internal answer-confidence, elicit verbalized confidence, and quantify mismatch cases (verbally confident but internally uncertain = overclaiming). Report an 'overclaiming rate'.

**Why it matters:** Operationalizes a slice of honesty as a concrete metric using only open weights and one GPU, no training. Overclaiming-rate is an interpretable, counterfactual honesty signal that complements behavioral truthfulness benchmarks.

**Relevant context:** honesty_faithfulness measure-honesty open problem; calibration / verbalized-confidence literature; linear probing for confidence; TruthfulQA/SimpleQA-style tasks.

# Self-BLEU vs. Embedding Diversity: Do Hivemind Conclusions Depend on the Metric?

**Problem:** Homogeneity studies use varied diversity metrics (distinct-n, self-BLEU, embedding cosine, Vendi). It is unclear whether the Hivemind conclusions are metric-robust or partly artifacts of surface-level metrics that miss semantic convergence (or vice versa).

**Direction:** Replicate the core inter-model homogeneity result on one open-ended prompt set across 8-10 open models, but compute homogeneity under multiple metrics in parallel (n-gram overlap, self-BLEU, sentence-embedding cosine, Vendi score). Twist: report where metrics agree/disagree and identify cases of high surface diversity but high semantic convergence (paraphrased sameness) — the most dangerous, least-visible homogeneity.

**Why it matters:** A methodological replication that tells the field which cheap metrics actually detect dangerous semantic homogeneity. Strengthens all downstream concentration-risk monitoring; needs only open models and standard libraries.

**Relevant context:** Metric-robustness replication of Artificial Hivemind (arXiv:2510.22954); grounded in the diversity-metric literature (Vendi, self-BLEU, SemScore arXiv:2401.17072).

# Structure-Aware Diversity Pursuit: Replicating a Homogenization Defense on Open Models

**Problem:** A 2026 paper frames structure-aware diversity pursuit as an AI-safety strategy against homogenization. Such defenses need independent replication on accessible open models to verify they actually reduce correlated failure rather than just surface variety.

**Direction:** Replicate the core diversity-promoting intervention from the structure-aware diversity work in a lightweight inference-time form on 4-6 open models, then measure whether it reduces *inter-model* homogeneity and shared-error rate on a small task. Twist: evaluate the accuracy cost (the open problem of 'diversity without sacrificing accuracy') to see whether the intervention is a free lunch or a trade-off.

**Why it matters:** Directly addresses the subfield's open problem of diversity-promoting objectives that don't sacrifice accuracy, via a reproducible, lab-independent test of a proposed safety defense.

**Relevant context:** Replicates 'Structure-Aware Diversity Pursuit as an AI Safety Strategy against Homogenization' (arXiv:2601.06116) on open models; ties to the Hivemind diversity-objective open problem.

# Does Fine-Tuning a Shared Base Inherit Its Blind Spots? A LoRA Replication

**Problem:** Concentration risk argues that downstream systems built on the same foundation model inherit its blind spots. This is asserted but rarely demonstrated cheaply: do several different fine-tunes of one open base retain correlated failures from the base?

**Direction:** Take one open base model and a few of its existing community fine-tunes (or train 2-3 small LoRA adapters on different small datasets — within a few hours on one GPU), then replicate error-correlation/homogeneity measurement among the fine-tunes and against the base. Twist: test whether the shared base's specific errors persist across all its descendants regardless of fine-tuning data.

**Why it matters:** Demonstrating inherited correlated failures from a shared base is the concrete mechanism behind foundation-model concentration risk — a key open problem. Small LoRA fine-tunes stay within the consumer-GPU/few-hours budget.

**Relevant context:** Replicates the 'shared foundationality causes correlated failures' claim (Correlated Errors arXiv:2506.07962; International AI Safety Report 2026) using one open base + lightweight LoRA fine-tunes.

# Hivemind in Tool/Function Calling: Do Agents Pick the Same Wrong Action?

**Problem:** Agentic deployments rely on models choosing tools/actions. If many models converge on the same incorrect or unsafe action in ambiguous situations, agent ensembles share blind spots — an under-studied homogeneity domain as agents proliferate.

**Direction:** Replicate homogeneity measurement on a function-calling/tool-selection task: present 6-8 open tool-capable models with ambiguous or trap scenarios (where the safe action differs from the obvious one) and record their chosen actions. Twist: measure the rate at which models jointly pick the same unsafe action vs. independence, and whether same-lineage models agree on wrong actions more.

**Why it matters:** Agentic systems are the near-future deployment surface; correlated unsafe action selection is a systemic risk for agent fleets. A reproducible evaluation built from public tool-use scenarios, no lab infrastructure needed.

**Relevant context:** Applies Artificial Hivemind homogeneity framing (arXiv:2510.22954) to tool/function-calling; uses open function-calling models and hand-built ambiguous-action scenarios.

# Replicating Hivemind with Infinity-Chat on Models the Paper Didn't Test

**Problem:** Infinity-Chat (26K queries, 31K annotations) is released, but the original study covered a specific model set. The newest open releases (post-paper) and certain underrepresented families weren't included — and homogeneity may differ for them.

**Direction:** Directly reuse the released Infinity-Chat benchmark and its evaluation protocol to run a fresh set of open models the paper did not cover (latest small open releases, non-Western open models, MoE small models). Twist: position these new models in the paper's homogeneity space — are recent releases joining the existing cluster, forming a new one, or genuinely more diverse?

**Why it matters:** A faithful, low-risk replication that extends the Best Paper's coverage and tests whether homogeneity is a stable, growing phenomenon. Maximally reproducible (released benchmark + open models), an ideal first hands-on safety project.

**Relevant context:** Direct replication using the released Infinity-Chat benchmark from Artificial Hivemind (arXiv:2510.22954), extended to an updated/under-covered open-model set.

# Does Sampling N Times From One Model Cover the Herd? Intra- vs Inter-Model Diversity

**Problem:** Artificial Hivemind reports both intra-model repetition and inter-model homogeneity. A practical question for diversity-as-defense: does drawing many samples from ONE model cover as much of the answer space as one sample from MANY models — or is the herd genuinely broader?

**Direction:** Replicate diversity measurement two ways on the same prompts: (a) N samples from a single open model, (b) one sample each from N open models. Compare answer-space coverage (embedding-space convex hull / Vendi score / unique-cluster count). Twist: quantify the marginal diversity gained from adding models vs. adding samples — directly informing whether multi-vendor ensembles add real diversity.

**Why it matters:** If many models barely out-cover one model's samples, the 'use multiple providers for robustness' assumption collapses — a sharp, decision-relevant result about concentration risk, produced with pure inference.

**Relevant context:** Operationalizes the intra- vs inter-model distinction from Artificial Hivemind (arXiv:2510.22954) using standard diversity metrics; open models only.

# Correlated Hallucinations: Do Models Confabulate the Same Fake Facts?

**Problem:** If models hallucinate *independently*, cross-checking among models catches errors; if they hallucinate the *same* fabricated fact, cross-model verification fails. Whether hallucinations are correlated (a homogeneity question) is under-measured.

**Direction:** Replicate error-correlation methodology specifically on hallucination: pose questions with verifiable answers (including some designed to induce confabulation, e.g. fake-entity questions) to 6-8 open models, and measure whether their *wrong* answers coincide on the same fabricated content. Twist: distinguish 'shared refusal/uncertainty' from 'shared specific fabrication' — the latter being the dangerous, verification-defeating case.

**Why it matters:** Cross-model agreement is a popular hallucination-detection heuristic; correlated hallucinations would silently break it. A reproducible, lab-independent measurement of a concrete systemic blind spot.

**Relevant context:** Replicates error-correlation analysis (Correlated Errors arXiv:2506.07962) focused on hallucination, with a shared-fabrication twist linking to Hivemind blind spots.

# SafetyInfinity: a safety-refusal slice of Infinity-Chat for measuring shared refusal blind spots

**Problem:** Infinity-Chat measures open-ended homogeneity on creative queries, but it does not isolate safety-relevant prompts. We do not know whether the Artificial Hivemind effect extends to safety behaviors: do independently trained models share the SAME refusal boundaries, so that a single ambiguous-harm prompt is mis-handled identically by all of them?

**Direction:** Curate ~150 borderline safety prompts (dual-use, ambiguous self-harm, gray-area persuasion) reusing Infinity-Chat's taxonomy structure. Query 8-12 open-weight chat models (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma, Phi, DeepSeek-distill) via a single consumer GPU or hosted APIs. Score each response as refuse/comply/partial with a simple LLM-judge plus manual spot-check. Compute an agreement-beyond-chance statistic (CAPA-style) on the refuse/comply decision to quantify how correlated refusal blind spots are. Release the prompt slice and per-model labels as a reusable mini-benchmark.

**Why it matters:** If safety boundaries are homogeneous, then deploying multiple 'diverse' models as defense-in-depth gives a false sense of redundancy — one adversarial prompt clears all of them at once. Quantifying correlated refusal failures is a concrete systemic-risk measurement that needs no lab infrastructure and is exactly the kind of long-horizon, diffuse-reward evaluation frontier labs under-invest in.

**Relevant context:** Extends the Artificial Hivemind / Infinity-Chat benchmark (NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper, arXiv:2510.22954) to the safety domain — listed explicitly in the subfield's generation hints (FR67/FR68: test safety-relevant domains, shared blind spots). CAPA chance-adjusted agreement metric from 'Great Models Think Alike' (arXiv:2502.04313).

# CAPA-for-refusals: an open tool to measure chance-adjusted agreement of safety decisions across models

**Problem:** The CAPA metric ('Great Models Think Alike') was designed for accuracy on multiple-choice tasks where a ground-truth answer exists. There is no standard, easy-to-use tool to compute chance-adjusted error correlation for binary SAFETY decisions (refuse vs comply), where there is no objective ground truth and the relevant 'failure' is jointly mis-handling a prompt.

**Direction:** Implement a small Python library that takes a matrix of model x prompt refuse/comply labels and outputs (a) pairwise chance-adjusted agreement, (b) a model-similarity dendrogram, and (c) a 'redundancy score' estimating how much independent safety coverage an ensemble actually provides. Validate it on the SafetyInfinity labels and a public refusal benchmark. Ship as a pip-installable package with a notebook.

**Why it matters:** Provides reusable infrastructure for anyone (auditors, small labs, regulators) to measure whether a 'diverse' model stack truly reduces correlated safety failure — directly serving the open problem of monitoring concentration/systemic risk across multiple deployed systems. High counterfactual value: it is tooling labs are unlikely to build because it scrutinizes the redundancy claims they market.

**Relevant context:** Adapts CAPA from arXiv:2502.04313 to the no-ground-truth refusal setting. Targets the subfield open problem of 'monitoring approaches for systemic/concentration risks that span multiple deployed systems' (EU AI Act systemic risk).

# JailbreakTransfer-Bench: measuring how correlated jailbreak susceptibility is across open models

**Problem:** It is folklore that jailbreaks 'transfer' across models, but there is no clean, reproducible benchmark quantifying the CORRELATION structure: given a set of jailbreak prompts and a set of models, how concentrated is the joint-failure probability? Homogeneity research has not connected the Hivemind framing to adversarial robustness.

**Direction:** Take 50-100 public jailbreak templates from existing repos (e.g., AdvBench-style, in-the-wild collections), apply each to 8-10 open-weight models on a single GPU, label success/failure with a harmfulness judge. Build a model x jailbreak success matrix and compute joint-failure probabilities and a 'monoculture index' (how often a jailbreak that beats model A also beats model B). Compare same-family vs cross-family pairs to test whether shared lineage drives correlated vulnerability.

**Why it matters:** A high monoculture index means an attacker who finds one exploit compromises the whole ecosystem — the canonical systemic risk. Quantifying it provides the empirical basis for arguing that genuine architectural/data diversity (not just multiple vendors) is needed for robustness. Uses only public artifacts and consumer compute.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'foundationality' / correlated-failure findings (arXiv:2404.09932) and reports that the same jailbreaks transfer across LLMs; extends Hivemind homogeneity to adversarial robustness, a flagged follow-up (shared blind spots).

# A steering slice of control-monitoring: can adding a 'deception' probe-direction as a TRIPWIRE catch alignment-faking without false alarms?

**Problem:** Control needs reliable misalignment monitors; concept-steering provides directions. Sub-problem: if we treat a learned 'deception' concept direction as a real-time tripwire (alarm when projection exceeds a threshold), what false-positive rate does it incur on benign-but-strategic conversations (negotiation, persuasion) that look superficially deceptive?

**Direction:** Decompose monitor reliability into a false-positive characterization. Extract a deception direction on a small open model, then run it as a threshold tripwire over a mix of (a) actual alignment-faking transcripts and (b) benign strategic dialogues. Plot the ROC and identify which benign behaviors trigger false alarms.

**Why it matters:** A monitor's usefulness is determined by its false-positive behavior on benign edge cases — exactly the unglamorous, counterfactual work labs underpublish. Open weights, one GPU, no training. The benign-trigger taxonomy is a directly useful deliverable for anyone deploying activation monitors.

**Relevant context:** SycophantSee activation diagnostics (Apart); ai_control activation-monitoring open problem; Beaglehole et al. probes outperforming judges; deception/alignment-faking transcripts.

# ForecastMonoculture: a benchmark for correlated errors of LLMs as predictors

**Problem:** Recent work shows GPT-4o, Claude and Gemini make highly correlated forecasting errors, acting like 'a single oracle with noise'. But there is no open, replicable benchmark or tool that lets a small researcher measure this correlation for any set of (including open-weight) models on resolvable questions.

**Direction:** Assemble ~200 already-resolved binary forecasting questions (past events with known outcomes, e.g., from public prediction-market archives). Query 6-10 models for probabilistic answers, score Brier/log loss, and compute the correlation matrix of their ERRORS (not just answers). Release a tool that estimates 'effective number of independent forecasters' in an LLM panel and tests whether averaging diverse models actually reduces error or just averages a shared bias.

**Why it matters:** As AI systems get used for high-stakes forecasting and decision support, correlated errors mean society's 'AI advisors' all blunder together — a diffuse, long-horizon systemic risk. Measuring effective diversity of model panels is exactly the under-served evaluation that needs no lab resources. Directly informs concentration-risk monitoring.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'The Oracle's Fingerprint: Correlated AI Forecasting Errors' (arXiv:2605.00844) and the Hivemind inter-model homogeneity result. Concentration-risk monitoring is a listed open problem (International AI Safety Report 2026).

# Reasoning-Hivemind: do reasoning models converge MORE or LESS than base chat models?

**Problem:** The Artificial Hivemind paper studied chat models; the subfield hints explicitly flag 'study homogeneity in reasoning models' as an open follow-up. It is unknown whether long chain-of-thought makes models diverge (more exploration) or converge harder (everyone finds the same 'optimal' path).

**Direction:** Pick ~80 open-ended and reasoning-flavored prompts from Infinity-Chat plus a few puzzle/strategy tasks. Compare a set of reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-distill, QwQ, o-style open models) against their non-reasoning siblings on the same consumer GPU. Measure both intra-model repetition (sample each prompt many times) and inter-model homogeneity using embedding-similarity and n-gram diversity metrics from the Hivemind paper. Report whether reasoning increases or collapses diversity.

**Why it matters:** If reasoning models converge on identical solution strategies, then a flaw in 'the' canonical reasoning chain is a shared blind spot across the whole reasoning ecosystem — a worsening systemic risk as reasoning models are deployed for agentic/high-stakes tasks. Cheap to run, directly answers a flagged open problem.

**Relevant context:** Direct follow-up named in subfield hints (study reasoning models). Grounded in Hivemind (arXiv:2510.22954) and CoT-homogenization observations ('Reasoning Models Generate Societies of Thought', arXiv:2601.10825).

# RefusalDiversity-Meter: quantifying how identical models' refusal *wordings* are

**Problem:** Beyond whether models refuse, the Hivemind effect predicts they refuse with strikingly similar LANGUAGE ('I cannot assist with that...'). No tool measures lexical/semantic homogeneity of refusal templates across providers, yet templated refusals are precisely what attackers fingerprint and optimize against.

**Direction:** Collect refusals from 8-12 models on a fixed set of harmful prompts, embed them, and compute pairwise semantic similarity plus shared-n-gram statistics. Build a small dashboard reporting a 'refusal homogeneity index' and the most-shared refusal phrases. Test whether refusal language is MORE homogeneous than ordinary helpful answers (a sign of shared alignment-tuning lineage).

**Why it matters:** Homogeneous refusal language is a shared attack surface (one universal refusal-suppression suffix works everywhere) and a measurable proxy for how much models share an alignment pipeline. It is a concrete, cheap measurement of the concentration of alignment methods — a systemic risk regulators care about. Needs no training.

**Relevant context:** Extends Hivemind inter-model homogeneity (arXiv:2510.22954) to refusal text; connects to refusal-pattern alignment via cross-model distillation (arXiv:2406.11285).

# Distillation-Lineage Detector: can we measure how 'related' two models are from outputs alone?

**Problem:** Systemic risk depends on hidden behavioral dependencies (shared pretraining data, distillation, alignment). But a downstream user deploying a 'diverse' multi-vendor stack has no black-box tool to detect that two models are actually distillation cousins with correlated failures.

**Direction:** Build a black-box similarity profiler: query a battery of probe prompts (idiosyncratic completions, tie-breaking choices, error patterns) across models, then cluster models by output fingerprint. Test whether the clustering recovers known lineage (e.g., distilled-from-GPT vs Llama-derived) on open models with documented provenance, establishing the tool as a lineage/relatedness estimator.

**Why it matters:** Lets auditors and procurement teams verify that a multi-model ensemble is genuinely independent before relying on it for redundancy — directly addressing correlated-failure systemic risk with a deployable, lab-independent tool. Model-organism-style probing scoped to 30h.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'How Independent are Large Language Models? A Statistical Framework for Auditing Behavioral Entanglement' (arXiv:2604.07650) and foundationality (arXiv:2404.09932). Serves the open problem of monitoring shared blind spots.

# EnsembleRedundancy-Bench: how much real safety coverage does adding a 2nd model buy?

**Problem:** Defense-in-depth assumes that stacking a second guard model catches what the first misses. If models are homogeneous, the marginal coverage of each added model collapses. No benchmark measures the diminishing-returns curve of safety-classifier ensembles built from independent models.

**Direction:** Use a public harmful/benign prompt set. Treat 6-10 open models as binary safety classifiers. Compute the coverage curve: catch rate of 1 model, best 2, best 3... and the marginal gain per added model. Compare against a hypothetical 'independent classifiers' baseline (predicted by error rates if uncorrelated). Quantify the 'redundancy gap' — how far short real ensembles fall of the independence ideal.

**Why it matters:** Gives builders of monitoring/guardrail stacks a concrete metric for whether their ensemble is real defense or correlated theater, and quantifies systemic over-reliance on a homogeneous model population. Pure evaluation, consumer compute, high counterfactual value (scrutinizes a marketing claim).

**Relevant context:** Operationalizes correlated-failure concerns from Hivemind and 'Great Models Think Alike' (arXiv:2502.04313) into a deployment-relevant ensemble-coverage benchmark; ties to AEGIS-style ensemble safety (arXiv:2404.05993).

# ValueHivemind: measuring convergence of moral/value judgments across models

**Problem:** Homogeneity work has focused on creative text. Whether independently trained models share the SAME value judgments on contested moral dilemmas is unmeasured — yet a shared moral blind spot deployed across many advice systems is a serious diffuse risk.

**Direction:** Assemble ~120 contested value-laden scenarios (trolley-style, political-economy tradeoffs, cultural-norm conflicts) with no consensus answer. Query 8-12 models, capture their chosen stance and justification. Measure inter-model agreement beyond chance and embedding homogeneity of justifications. Test whether models converge on a single 'corporate-aligned' value profile and where they all share the same blind spots (e.g., systematically ignoring a minority perspective).

**Why it matters:** If billions of users get advice from value-homogeneous models, society's moral diversity narrows and shared moral blind spots become systemic. Measuring value monoculture is a long-horizon, fuzzy-reward problem frontier labs deprioritize and needs no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Extends Hivemind (arXiv:2510.22954) to value judgments; connects to 'Homogenizing Effect of LLMs on Human Expression and Thought' (arXiv:2508.01491). Addresses shared-blind-spot follow-up (FR68).

# TemperatureRescue: does sampling diversity actually break the Hivemind, or just reshuffle it?

**Problem:** A common assumed fix for output homogeneity is to raise temperature / use diverse decoding. But it is unmeasured whether high-temperature sampling produces GENUINELY diverse safety-relevant content or just lexical variation around the same underlying mode (and the same blind spots).

**Direction:** On a fixed set of prompts, sweep temperature and decoding strategies (top-p, min-p, typical) for several open models on one GPU. Distinguish surface diversity (n-gram/lexical) from semantic/decision diversity (does the refuse/comply or moral stance actually change?). Build a small tool reporting the gap between lexical and decision diversity as a function of decoding settings.

**Why it matters:** Tells practitioners whether decoding tricks are a real or illusory remedy for correlated failures — important because cheap decoding fixes are often proposed as substitutes for genuine model diversity. Pure inference, no training, directly tests a diversity-promoting claim.

**Relevant context:** Tests the Hivemind paper's intra-model repetition finding and the open problem of diversity-promoting methods that don't sacrifice accuracy (arXiv:2510.22954).

# MultilingualHivemind: are shared safety blind spots worse in low-resource languages?

**Problem:** Two findings collide and have not been combined: (a) models are homogeneous, and (b) safety alignment is much weaker in low-resource languages. If all models share the SAME multilingual weak spots, then a single low-resource-language jailbreak is a universal key.

**Direction:** Take ~60 harmful prompts, translate into 4-6 languages spanning resource levels (using a translation API or open MT). Query 6-8 multilingual open models, label refusal per language. Measure whether the safety gap in low-resource languages is correlated ACROSS models (shared blind spot) and compute a per-language monoculture index.

**Why it matters:** Correlated multilingual blind spots mean the entire model ecosystem is jailbreakable through the same linguistic side door — a concrete, under-measured global systemic risk. Cheap, lab-independent, and high counterfactual value (labs focus alignment effort on English).

**Relevant context:** Combines Hivemind homogeneity with documented low-resource safety failures (Welo Data 'Global Security Blind Spots'; translation-as-jailbreak). Addresses shared-blind-spot follow-up.

# Self-Correction-Monoculture: do all models share the same self-correction blind spot?

**Problem:** Self-Correction Bench found LLMs fail to fix their OWN errors while fixing identical external errors. It is unknown whether this blind spot is homogeneous — i.e., whether all models fail to self-correct on the SAME items, making the failure systemic rather than idiosyncratic.

**Direction:** Reuse/replicate a small self-correction probe set on 6-10 open models. For each item, record whether each model self-corrects. Compute the joint failure structure: are the items that model A can't self-correct the same ones model B can't? Report a self-correction monoculture index and whether cross-model checking (A reviews B) escapes the blind spot.

**Why it matters:** If self-correction blind spots are shared, then pipelines that use one model to review another inherit the same blind spot — undermining a core AI-oversight safety mechanism. Quantifies a correlated-failure risk in oversight with consumer compute and public methods.

**Relevant context:** Builds on 'Self-Correction Bench' (arXiv:2507.02778) and connects to the AI-oversight correlated-failure thesis of 'Great Models Think Alike' (arXiv:2502.04313).

# HivemindDrift: tracking whether successive model releases are converging over time

**Problem:** Concentration risk grows if each new model generation is MORE homogeneous than the last. There is no longitudinal tool measuring whether the model population is converging or diversifying across release cohorts.

**Direction:** Curate a fixed homogeneity probe set. Run it across a chronological set of open models spanning ~2 years of releases (e.g., Llama-2 -> Llama-3 -> newer, plus contemporaneous Qwen/Mistral cohorts). Compute inter-model homogeneity per cohort and plot the trend over time. Release the probe set and a reproducible script so the measurement can be re-run on future releases.

**Why it matters:** A rising convergence trend is direct evidence that the ecosystem is heading toward a riskier monoculture — exactly the kind of systemic-risk indicator regulators and the AI Safety Report want but no one is tracking. Reusable, lab-independent, longitudinal infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Operationalizes the Hivemind inter-model homogeneity metric as a time series; supports concentration-risk monitoring (International AI Safety Report 2026).

# Decomposing 'realistic sycophancy evaluation' into a multi-turn pressure-escalation slice using real conversation structure

**Problem:** Standard sycophancy benchmarks overstate robustness (Claude Opus 4.5: 10% course-correction under real pressure). The decomposable sub-problem: how does sycophancy scale with the NUMBER of pushback turns — is there a turn-count threshold at which open models capitulate, and is that threshold shared across models?

**Direction:** Decompose realistic sycophancy into an escalation-curve experiment. Build multi-turn dialogues where a user repeatedly pushes back on a correct answer; measure capitulation rate as a function of pushback turns across several open models. Cross-reference with homogeneity: do models share the same capitulation threshold?

**Why it matters:** Realistic, multi-turn sycophancy evaluation is an explicit methodology gap, and capitulation-vs-turns is a vivid, communicable curve. Open models, single GPU, no training. The shared-threshold angle adds a systemic-risk dimension labs rarely test on open models.

**Relevant context:** Claude Opus 4.5 system card sycophancy-under-pressure (10% course-correction); honesty_faithfulness realistic-sycophancy gap; Infinity-Chat / real-conversation structure; homogeneity of capitulation.

# AgentMonoculture-Sim: a tiny sandbox for cascading failures in same-model agent swarms

**Problem:** Monoculture-collapse theory predicts that multi-agent systems built on the same base model share correlated vulnerabilities, causing cascades. There is no small, runnable testbed for a beginner to OBSERVE and MEASURE such a cascade.

**Direction:** Build a minimal multi-agent simulation (5-10 agents passing messages on a simple cooperative task) where all agents use the same open model vs a mixed-model condition. Inject a poisoned/ambiguous input and measure how far the failure propagates (fraction of agents that adopt the wrong belief/action) in the homogeneous vs heterogeneous swarm. Ship the sandbox as a notebook.

**Why it matters:** Provides concrete, reproducible evidence and infrastructure for the cascading-failure open problem, letting researchers study correlated-failure propagation without lab-scale systems. Strategically valuable monitoring/sandbox infra scoped to a small prototype.

**Relevant context:** Grounds 'monoculture collapse' / cascading reliability failures (Risk Analysis Techniques for Governed LLM Multi-Agent Systems, arXiv:2508.05687) into a runnable testbed. Cascading-failure characterization is a listed open problem.

# BlindSpotMiner: an automated tool to surface prompts where ALL models fail together

**Problem:** We lack tooling to actively SEARCH for inputs that trigger correlated failure across many models — the high-value 'universal blind spots'. Current homogeneity work measures average similarity but doesn't mine the worst-case shared-failure prompts.

**Direction:** Implement a simple search loop: start from a seed prompt set, score each prompt by how many of N models fail/agree-wrongly on it, then mutate (paraphrase, add context) the highest-correlation prompts to amplify joint failure. Output a ranked list of 'universal blind spot' prompts. Use cheap open models so the whole loop runs on one GPU. Characterize what these prompts have in common.

**Why it matters:** Universal blind spots are the single points of failure of the model ecosystem; a tool that finds them turns diffuse systemic risk into concrete, fixable test cases. Counterfactually valuable as an open auditing tool labs would not prioritize building against themselves.

**Relevant context:** Inspired by quality-diversity vulnerability discovery (arXiv:2606.00801) and Hivemind shared-blind-spot framing; serves the open problem of monitoring shared blind spots across deployed systems.

# PersonaHivemind: do role/persona prompts collapse to the same character across models?

**Problem:** Practitioners use system-prompt personas to differentiate assistants, assuming this yields behavioral diversity. It is unmeasured whether the same persona prompt produces a homogeneous character across different base models — and whether persona-induced behaviors share blind spots.

**Direction:** Define ~10 persona system prompts (cautious advisor, blunt expert, etc.). For each persona, query several open models on a fixed task set. Measure inter-model homogeneity within each persona vs the no-persona baseline. Test whether personas amplify or reduce the Hivemind effect, and whether 'unsafe' personas jailbreak all models equally.

**Why it matters:** If personas are skin-deep over a shared latent character, then product 'diversity' built on personas is illusory and shares the same safety failures — relevant to deployers who think persona variety buys robustness. Inference-only, lab-independent.

**Relevant context:** Extends Hivemind homogeneity (arXiv:2510.22954) to persona-conditioned generation; novel combination not in the catalogue's obvious framings.

# HivemindHarm-Index: a single deployable metric for an LLM panel's correlated-failure risk

**Problem:** There is no compact, standardized score a deployer can compute to summarize how risky their specific set of models is from a correlated-failure standpoint. Researchers report many ad-hoc similarity numbers; deployers need one actionable index.

**Direction:** Define a composite 'Correlated-Failure Risk Index' combining (1) chance-adjusted error agreement, (2) joint-failure probability on a safety probe set, and (3) effective number of independent models. Implement as a tool that ingests a panel's outputs and emits the index plus the dominant shared-failure cluster. Calibrate on several open-model panels and show it discriminates same-family from mixed panels.

**Why it matters:** Turns abstract homogeneity research into a procurement/governance-ready metric for systemic risk — exactly what EU AI Act systemic-risk monitoring needs and what no lab provides for its competitors' stacks. Pure analysis, high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Synthesizes CAPA (arXiv:2502.04313), Hivemind homogeneity, and effective-independence ideas into a governance metric; addresses the systemic-risk monitoring open problem.

# CodeHivemind: do models generate the same insecure code patterns?

**Problem:** Homogeneity in code generation is safety-critical: if all coding assistants emit the SAME insecure idiom for a given task, that vulnerability propagates across all software built with AI assistance. This shared-blind-spot dimension is unmeasured in the Hivemind framing.

**Direction:** Take ~50 coding tasks known to have a secure/insecure choice (SQL queries, crypto usage, input validation). Query 6-10 open code models. Detect whether they converge on the same insecure pattern using simple static checks. Measure inter-model homogeneity of the vulnerability and whether the 'popular wrong answer' is shared. Release task set and per-model labels.

**Why it matters:** Correlated insecure-code generation means AI-assisted software develops a monoculture of the same bugs — an at-scale, long-horizon systemic risk to the software supply chain. Static-check scoring keeps it within beginner skills and consumer compute.

**Relevant context:** Extends Hivemind to the code domain (named extension direction: test safety-relevant domains); connects shared-blind-spot risk to software supply chain.

# DiversityFloor: how few prompts do you need to expose the Hivemind? A sample-efficiency benchmark

**Problem:** Running full homogeneity audits (thousands of prompts x dozens of models) is expensive. Auditors need to know the minimal probe set that reliably estimates a model panel's homogeneity — but no work characterizes the sample efficiency of homogeneity measurement.

**Direction:** Using a labeled homogeneity dataset (e.g., the SafetyInfinity slice), subsample prompts and models and measure how the estimated homogeneity index converges with probe-set size. Identify a small 'core probe set' that approximates the full estimate. Release the core probe set as a cheap audit kit.

**Why it matters:** Makes systemic-risk auditing affordable for small actors and regulators, lowering the barrier to routine concentration-risk monitoring. Methodologically simple (subsampling + statistics), fits beginner stats skills, and produces reusable infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Methodological tooling on top of the Hivemind/Infinity-Chat benchmark; serves the systemic-risk monitoring open problem with a practical efficiency angle.

# OversightLeakage-Bench: when a judge model shares lineage with the model it grades

**Problem:** 'Great Models Think Alike' showed LLM judges favor models similar to themselves. There is no easy benchmark letting a researcher measure, for a chosen judge and a set of graded models, how much the judge's scores are biased by similarity — a key flaw in AI-oversight pipelines.

**Direction:** Set up an LLM-as-judge over outputs from several open models on open-ended tasks. Compute each graded model's similarity to the judge (via the lineage/fingerprint probe) and correlate it with the judge's score advantage. Repeat across a few judges. Build a tool that reports a 'self-preference / similarity-bias' coefficient for any judge configuration.

**Why it matters:** Homogeneity silently corrupts automated evaluation and oversight; a tool to detect similarity bias in judge pipelines protects the integrity of scalable oversight — a core safety mechanism. Inference-only, public models, high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Directly operationalizes the self-preference/similarity-bias result of 'Great Models Think Alike' (arXiv:2502.04313) into a reusable benchmark for the AI-oversight failure mode.

# QuantizationHivemind: does quantization make models converge or diverge?

**Problem:** Deployers run quantized variants (4-bit, 8-bit) to save compute. It is unmeasured whether quantization homogenizes outputs (collapsing toward a shared mode and shared blind spots) or introduces idiosyncratic divergence — relevant because most real deployments are quantized.

**Direction:** Take 2-3 open models, run full-precision vs several quantization levels on a fixed homogeneity/safety probe set on one GPU. Measure intra-model repetition and the model's distance from its full-precision self, plus whether different quantized models converge toward each other. Report quantization's effect on homogeneity and on refusal blind spots.

**Why it matters:** If quantization amplifies shared blind spots, the deployed (quantized) ecosystem is even more of a monoculture than benchmark numbers (run at full precision) suggest — a measurement gap with direct deployment relevance. Perfectly sized for a single consumer GPU.

**Relevant context:** Novel extension of the Hivemind effect to the quantization axis; uses standard open quantization tooling. Addresses deployment-realistic systemic-risk measurement.

# HumanVsHive: calibrating model homogeneity against actual human-answer diversity

**Problem:** Reports that models are 'homogeneous' lack a human baseline on the same prompts. Infinity-Chat has 25 human annotations per example — a chance to quantify exactly how much LESS diverse models are than humans, which no compact tool reports.

**Direction:** Use the public Infinity-Chat human annotations as the human-diversity reference. Generate model answers for a matched subset, compute the same diversity metrics for the human set and each model set, and report a 'diversity deficit ratio' (human diversity / model diversity). Build it into a small reusable evaluator.

**Why it matters:** A calibrated human baseline transforms 'models are similar' into 'models are N times less diverse than people' — a far more compelling and policy-relevant statement about homogenization of thought. Reuses an existing public dataset; no training, modest compute.

**Relevant context:** Directly leverages Infinity-Chat's 31K human annotations (arXiv:2510.22954); connects to homogenization-of-human-thought concern (arXiv:2508.01491).

# DomainBlindSpot-Bench: does homogeneity concentrate in specific high-stakes domains?

**Problem:** Homogeneity is likely uneven — models may be diverse on casual chat but identical on, say, medical or legal caution. No benchmark maps WHERE in topic space the Hivemind is strongest, yet that is exactly where shared blind spots matter most.

**Direction:** Organize prompts into high-stakes domains (medical advice, legal, financial, mental-health, security). Measure inter-model homogeneity per domain across 6-10 open models and rank domains by homogeneity. Identify the 'most monocultural' high-stakes domain and characterize the shared default response. Release a domain-tagged probe set.

**Why it matters:** Pinpoints where correlated failures would do the most societal harm, prioritizing safety effort on the highest-homogeneity high-stakes domains. A targeted measurement gap; cheap and lab-independent, serving long-horizon systemic-risk concerns.

**Relevant context:** Refines Hivemind (arXiv:2510.22954) along a domain axis (named extension: safety-relevant domains); supports concentration-risk monitoring across deployed systems.

# Token-Depth Mapping of Refusal Recovery

**Problem:** Qi et al. showed safety alignment is shallow, concentrated in the first few output tokens, but exactly how many tokens deep the refusal signal extends, and whether models can 'recover' (resume refusing) after a forced compliant prefix, is poorly characterized across open models.

**Direction:** Using prefilling attacks on open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B via a single GPU), force compliant prefixes of varying lengths (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 tokens) and measure at what prefix length the model can no longer recover and refuse. Plot a 'recovery curve' per model. No training needed — just inference with prefill control.

**Why it matters:** Quantifying the exact depth of shallow alignment and the recovery boundary gives a cheap, model-agnostic robustness metric. It directly tests the open problem of deepening alignment and provides a counterfactually valuable diagnostic any small lab can run without proprietary tooling.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946, ICLR 2025 Outstanding Paper): alignment adapts the generative distribution primarily over the first few tokens; prefilling attacks exploit this. Follow-up work (arXiv:2503.03710, arXiv:2512.05518) proposes 'deep' alignment where models recover after a compliant prefix. Recovery boundary as a function of prefix length is not systematically mapped.

# PromptSensitivity-Homogeneity: do all models break on the SAME prompt perturbations?

**Problem:** Models are known to be brittle to trivial prompt rephrasings. It is unmeasured whether this brittleness is correlated — i.e., whether the SAME rephrasing flips the behavior of all models simultaneously (a shared fragility) versus idiosyncratic per-model brittleness.

**Direction:** Take ~40 safety/decision prompts. Generate controlled perturbations (typos, reordering, polite framing, added authority). Query 6-10 open models and record behavior flips. Measure whether perturbations that flip model A also flip model B (correlated brittleness index). Release a perturbation toolkit and the flip matrix.

**Why it matters:** Correlated prompt-brittleness means a single innocuous-looking phrasing can simultaneously destabilize an entire fleet of deployed assistants — a measurable, under-explored systemic fragility. Simple to implement; consumer compute; high counterfactual value as open auditing infra.

**Relevant context:** Combines prompt-brittleness literature with Hivemind shared-blind-spot framing; novel angle on correlated failure not in the obvious catalogue framings.

# OpenVsClosed-Diversity: do open-weight derivatives inherit the same blind spots as their teachers?

**Problem:** Many open models are distilled from a few closed teachers. If open derivatives inherit the teachers' blind spots, the apparent diversity of the open ecosystem is illusory — a measurement no public tool provides.

**Direction:** Group open models by likely teacher lineage (GPT-distilled vs Llama-derived vs independently pretrained). On a shared safety/blind-spot probe set, measure within-lineage vs across-lineage homogeneity and whether within-lineage models fail jointly more often. Report an 'inherited blind spot' statistic. Use only black-box queries on open models.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies how much the open ecosystem's diversity is real vs inherited from a few proprietary teachers — central to the concentration-risk concern that 'few foundation model providers' drive systemic risk. Lab-independent and directly policy-relevant.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in foundationality / shared learned components (arXiv:2404.09932) and distillation-driven correlation; addresses the concentration-risk open problem (International AI Safety Report 2026).

# DiversityGain-Bench: does prompting for diversity recover human-level variety without losing accuracy?

**Problem:** Diversity-promoting methods that don't sacrifice accuracy is a named open problem. Cheap inference-time interventions (explicit 'give an unusual answer' prompts, diverse-decoding, persona rotation) are proposed but not benchmarked against accuracy on the same axis.

**Direction:** Build a small benchmark with both a diversity metric and a correctness/quality metric on tasks that have both an open-ended and a checkable component. Compare baseline vs several inference-time diversity interventions across a few open models. Plot the diversity-accuracy frontier and report which interventions buy diversity for free vs at a cost. Release the harness.

**Why it matters:** Gives practitioners an evidence-based, training-free recipe to reduce homogeneity (and thus correlated failure) without hurting quality — directly serving the diversity-without-accuracy-loss open problem at consumer scale. No training required, fully reproducible.

**Relevant context:** Targets the Hivemind extension 'diversity-promoting objectives that don't sacrifice accuracy' (arXiv:2510.22954), restricted to inference-time methods feasible in 30h.

# TieBreaker-Fingerprint: using forced-choice ties to measure latent model agreement

**Problem:** Standard homogeneity metrics rely on free-text similarity, which is noisy. There is no lightweight benchmark using forced binary/forced-ranking 'tie-break' decisions (where models have no quality reason to prefer either option) to expose shared latent biases cleanly.

**Direction:** Construct ~100 forced-choice items with two equally-valid options (A or B, order-randomized). Query many models. Because there is no correct answer, any cross-model agreement beyond 50% reveals a SHARED latent bias. Measure the agreement spectrum and identify the strongest shared biases. Package as a cheap, near-deterministic homogeneity probe.

**Why it matters:** Forced-tie probing is a clean, low-noise instrument for detecting hidden behavioral entanglement and shared biases — useful infrastructure for routine monoculture monitoring. Tiny compute, simple scoring, ideal for a beginner, and counterfactually valuable as open tooling.

**Relevant context:** Methodologically inspired by behavioral-entanglement auditing (arXiv:2604.07650) and CAPA chance-adjustment (arXiv:2502.04313); a fresh measurement instrument for the Hivemind effect.

# Do shared blind spots survive into safety-critical refusals? A refusal-overlap stress test

**Problem:** Prior work shows LLM refusal sets overlap heavily across vendors (e.g., when GPT-4.5 refuses, Claude refuses ~67% of the time; open models exceed 80% overlap). But it is unknown whether the *gaps* — prompts that ALL models wrongly comply with — are correlated, which would mean a single crafted-harmful prompt slips past every deployed guardrail simultaneously.

**Direction:** Assemble a few hundred borderline-harmful prompts (from public over-refusal/jailbreak datasets like FalseReject and 'Do Anything Now'). Query 6-8 open and API models. Build a per-prompt refusal matrix and measure: (1) the rate of unanimous *wrong* compliance, (2) whether compliance failures cluster on the same prompts more than chance (permutation test vs. an independence null). Characterize what topical features predict shared blind spots.

**Why it matters:** If high-stakes deployments each pick a different vendor for redundancy but all share the same compliance blind spots, the apparent diversity is illusory and a single attack generalizes. This directly tests the 'correlated failures across systems sharing blind spots' open problem with no training and only API/consumer-GPU inference.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in FalseReject (arXiv 2505.08054), refusal-overlap findings (Artificial Hivemind context), and the open problem on shared blind spots. Uses only public datasets and inference.

# Reproducing the Artificial Hivemind on safety-relevant open-ended prompts

**Problem:** The NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper found striking inter-model homogeneity on open-ended generation using Infinity-Chat, but its taxonomy emphasizes creative/brainstorm tasks. Whether the hivemind effect extends to *safety-relevant* open-ended prompts (e.g., 'list ways an AI could be misused', 'brainstorm risks of X', 'how could this go wrong') is untested.

**Direction:** Curate ~150 safety-flavored open-ended prompts (threat-modeling, red-team brainstorm, risk enumeration). Run 6-8 small/open models plus a couple of APIs. Reuse the paper's diversity metrics (embedding-based pairwise similarity for inter-model homogeneity, intra-model self-similarity). Compare hivemind strength on safety prompts vs. matched generic creative prompts.

**Why it matters:** If models converge on the SAME risk enumerations, our collective ability to brainstorm novel AI threats via LLMs has a systematic blind spot — everyone gets the same incomplete list. Quantifying this is a direct, feasible extension of the foundational paper.

**Relevant context:** Direct follow-up to Artificial Hivemind (OpenReview saDOrrnNTz), using its diversity-metric methodology and the Infinity-Chat-style prompt taxonomy. No training; embedding similarity runs on a single GPU.

# Does the hivemind tighten in reasoning models? Temperature and chain-of-thought as homogeneity amplifiers

**Problem:** The Artificial Hivemind paper noted reasoning models as an open follow-up. It is unclear whether explicit chain-of-thought *increases* inter-model homogeneity (because reasoning funnels models toward the same 'correct' path) or *decreases* it (because diverse reasoning chains diverge).

**Direction:** Take open reasoning-capable small models (e.g., distilled R1-style models, Qwen reasoning variants). On a fixed set of open-ended prompts, compare output diversity with reasoning on vs. off (and across temperatures). Measure inter-model embedding similarity in both conditions; test whether reasoning is a homogeneity amplifier.

**Why it matters:** Reasoning models are being deployed into high-stakes pipelines precisely because they 'think'. If reasoning collapses output diversity, redundancy among reasoning agents buys less safety than expected — a medium-horizon risk labs under-study.

**Relevant context:** Explicit follow-up suggested in the model_homogeneity context ('study homogeneity in reasoning models'). Uses open distilled reasoning models on a consumer GPU.

# Correlated errors at the failure tail: do the strongest models err together most?

**Problem:** Recent work (Correlated Errors in LLMs, arXiv 2506.07962) reports that larger, more accurate models have MORE correlated errors despite distinct providers — counterintuitive and safety-relevant. This surprising result deserves an independent, scoped replication on a fresh task suite.

**Direction:** Pick a multiple-choice safety/factual benchmark (e.g., a safety-knowledge subset, TruthfulQA-style items). Score 8-10 models spanning capability levels. For each pair, compute the conditional probability that both err on the same item vs. an independence baseline; regress error-correlation on average accuracy to test whether 'better models err together more'.

**Why it matters:** If capability gains import correlated errors, scaling makes ensembles and cross-checks *less* protective exactly as stakes rise. This is a counterintuitive, infrastructure-free finding worth confirming and communicating.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on Correlated Errors in LLMs (arXiv 2506.07962). Pure inference + statistics on a single GPU / API calls.

# Jailbreak transfer as a homogeneity meter: mapping shared vulnerability across an open-model family tree

**Problem:** Jailbreak transferability is argued to emerge from shared representations (arXiv 2506.12913). If true, the degree to which a jailbreak transfers between two models is a *behavioral measure of their homogeneity*. No one has used transfer rate as a similarity metric across a known lineage of open models.

**Direction:** Take a set of open models with known lineage (base + several fine-tunes/distillations, plus unrelated families). Use a small bank of published jailbreak prompts. Measure pairwise jailbreak transfer success and build a 'vulnerability dendrogram'. Test whether transfer rate tracks known lineage and whether shared base = shared vulnerability.

**Why it matters:** Provides a cheap, training-free probe for hidden model homogeneity that downstream deployers could use to audit whether their 'diverse' model pool actually shares attack surface — relevant to concentration risk monitoring.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on 'Jailbreak Transferability Emerges from Shared Representations' (arXiv 2506.12913) and the systemic reuse vulnerability framing. Uses public jailbreak prompts and open models only.

# The distilled-monoculture hypothesis: do high-distillation models share more failures?

**Problem:** Distillation-quantification work (arXiv 2501.12619) estimates that many open and closed models have high 'distillation degree' (sharing a teacher), while Claude/Gemini stand apart. If distillation drives homogeneity, high-distillation models should fail on the same items more than low-distillation ones — an untested prediction.

**Direction:** Group ~10 models into 'high-distillation' (likely sharing GPT-style teachers) vs. 'distinct lineage' clusters using the published distillation estimates. On a fixed error-prone benchmark, measure within-cluster vs. across-cluster error correlation. Test whether distillation lineage predicts correlated failure.

**Why it matters:** If distillation silently couples failure modes, the apparent diversity of the open-model ecosystem is overstated, and concentration risk hides behind nominally independent models. This is exactly the systemic-risk signal regulators want to monitor.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on Quantification of LLM Distillation (arXiv 2501.12619) and Correlated Errors (2506.07962). Inference + correlation analysis on a consumer GPU.

# Do Jailbreaks Lobotomize? Measuring Capability Tax of Successful Attacks

**Problem:** StrongREJECT found that jailbreaks which bypass safety fine-tuning tend to reduce the model's capabilities, but this 'capability tax' has not been systematically measured as a function of attack type, raising the question of whether some attacks elicit harmful but useless output.

**Direction:** For a fixed open model, apply several jailbreaks (prefill, refusal-direction ablation, many-shot, low-resource translation) and measure post-jailbreak performance on neutral capability benchmarks (GSM8K subset, MMLU subset) administered within the jailbroken context. Compare each attack's capability degradation against its StrongREJECT willingness score.

**Why it matters:** If the strongest willingness-inducing attacks also cause the most capability loss, the real-world threat is overstated and benchmarks should report a willingness-vs-capability tradeoff. This reframes how robustness is evaluated — a diffuse, fuzzy-reward measurement problem ideal for outside-lab work, needing no training.

**Relevant context:** StrongREJECT (Souly et al., arXiv:2402.10260, NeurIPS 2024): jailbreaks bypassing safety fine-tuning tend to reduce capabilities; prior evaluators overstate effectiveness by ignoring response quality. The capability tax per attack type and its correlation with willingness is unmeasured.

# Family bias in LLM-as-judge: a self-favoring monoculture stress test for evaluation pipelines

**Problem:** LLM judges favor their own and same-family outputs (self-preference and family bias; arXiv 2410.21819). Safety pipelines increasingly use one model family both to generate and to judge. If the judge systematically inflates same-family safety outputs, automated safety evals are silently biased toward the provider's own model.

**Direction:** Generate responses to a fixed safety-eval prompt set from 4-6 model families. Have each family's model judge ALL responses on a safety rubric. Compute the same-family score inflation (judge's rating of own-family vs. cross-family, controlling for an external human/aggregate gold). Quantify how much a monoculture eval setup distorts safety rankings.

**Why it matters:** Concentration on one provider for both generation and evaluation creates a self-grading loop that overstates safety. Demonstrating the size of this bias warns deployers against single-vendor safety eval stacks — a counterfactually valuable audit needing no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge (arXiv 2410.21819) and family-bias findings. Uses API/open models and a public safety rubric; no training.

# Verifier-ensemble illusion: how much redundancy do you actually buy from N 'independent' safety checkers?

**Problem:** Multi-model safety checks assume independence, but behavioral-entanglement audits (arXiv 2604.07650) show ostensibly independent models share synchronized failures. Practitioners size redundancy by counting models, not by their effective independence.

**Direction:** Build a small harness where N models each act as a binary safety classifier on a labeled harmful/benign prompt set. Estimate each pair's failure correlation, then compute the 'effective number of independent verifiers' (e.g., via the correlation-adjusted variance reduction) vs. the naive count N. Show how much the safety guarantee shrinks once correlation is accounted for.

**Why it matters:** Gives deployers a concrete, reusable formula+notebook to discount redundancy claims when their verifiers are homogeneous. Directly operationalizes the 'monitoring concentration risk across systems' open problem as a small infrastructure prototype.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on the behavioral-entanglement auditing framework (arXiv 2604.07650) and ensemble-diversity literature. Pure classification + statistics on a single GPU.

# Intra-model repetition as a hidden mode-collapse failure: measuring 'idea exhaustion' under resampling

**Problem:** The Artificial Hivemind paper documents intra-model repetition (one model keeps producing similar responses). The safety failure this implies — a model that exhausts its idea space after a few samples — is not quantified as a function of sample count, which matters for any safety process relying on diverse resampling (best-of-N, self-critique).

**Direction:** For each of several open models, resample K=50 outputs per open-ended/safety prompt at fixed temperature. Plot the growth of distinct semantic clusters (via embedding clustering) as K increases; fit a saturation curve and report the 'effective diversity ceiling'. Compare across models and prompt types.

**Why it matters:** If resampling saturates after ~5 ideas, best-of-N and diversity-based safety mechanisms hit a hard ceiling. Quantifying the ceiling tells safety engineers when more samples stop buying coverage — a clean, communicable finding.

**Relevant context:** Direct follow-up to the intra-model repetition result in Artificial Hivemind. Embedding clustering and resampling run on a consumer GPU.

# Shared hallucination: do independent models hallucinate the SAME false facts?

**Problem:** Homogeneity research focuses on style/refusals, but the most dangerous shared blind spot is shared *false confidence*. If models trained on overlapping corpora hallucinate identical wrong answers, cross-model agreement (a common reliability heuristic) becomes a false safety signal.

**Direction:** Use a set of questions designed to elicit hallucinations (obscure or fabricated entities, plausible-but-false claims). Query 8-10 models. Among incorrect answers, measure the rate at which multiple models give the *same wrong* answer vs. independently different wrong answers (string/semantic match). Quantify 'correlated hallucination'.

**Why it matters:** Agreement-based verification (asking several models and trusting consensus) silently fails when models share hallucinations. Demonstrating correlated hallucinations undermines a widely used cheap safety heuristic — high counterfactual value, no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Connects correlated-error findings (2506.07962) to hallucination; uses TruthfulQA-style and fabricated-entity prompts. Inference + matching only.

# Position and ordering blind spots shared across models: a correlated-bias incident study

**Problem:** Many models share systematic biases (e.g., position bias in multiple-choice, ordering bias in pairwise comparison). If these biases are correlated across vendors, a single adversarial reordering can flip decisions in every model at once — a shared exploitable failure mode.

**Direction:** On a fixed MCQ and pairwise-preference set, permute answer positions/order across models. Measure each model's position-bias magnitude and direction, then test whether biases are correlated across models (same option letter / same position favored). Estimate the fraction of items where a single reorder flips ALL models the same way.

**Why it matters:** Shared, predictable input-format biases mean an attacker needs to craft only one manipulation to fool a diverse model pool — directly demonstrating correlated, exploitable failure. Cheap to run, broadly relevant to eval and agentic safety.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on documented position/order biases in LLM evaluation and the correlated-failure framing. Public benchmarks + inference only.

# Tokenizer-shared failures: do models with the same tokenizer family break on the same inputs?

**Problem:** Homogeneity may have a low-level cause: shared tokenizers. Models using the same tokenizer (e.g., GPT-style BPE, Llama tokenizer) may share tokenization-induced failures (number splitting, rare-character glitches, 'glitch tokens'). Whether failure modes cluster by tokenizer is untested as a homogeneity driver.

**Direction:** Assemble inputs known to stress tokenization (long numbers, unusual unicode, glitch-token candidates). Group open models by tokenizer lineage. Measure failure rates and test whether same-tokenizer models fail on the same specific inputs more than cross-tokenizer pairs.

**Why it matters:** Identifies a concrete, mechanistic source of correlated failures that propagates across every model sharing a tokenizer — a supply-chain-style monoculture risk deployers never check. Fully open-model, no training.

**Relevant context:** Connects model_homogeneity 'shared blind spots' to tokenizer reuse; uses open models with documented tokenizers. Inference only on a consumer GPU.

# When does diversity collapse? Mapping the temperature/decoding boundary of inter-model homogeneity

**Problem:** Inter-model homogeneity is usually measured at default settings, but it is a boundary-condition question: at what decoding configuration (temperature, top-p) does homogeneity appear or vanish? Knowing the boundary tells us whether diversity can be cheaply recovered by sampling.

**Direction:** Hold prompts fixed; sweep temperature and top-p across several open models. At each setting measure inter-model pairwise similarity and intra-model diversity. Find the boundary where outputs stop converging, and test whether high-temperature 'diversity' is genuine (semantically distinct) or just surface noise.

**Why it matters:** If safety-relevant diversity can be recovered by turning up temperature, that is a cheap mitigation; if homogeneity is decoding-invariant, the problem is deeper. Either result is an actionable, communicable boundary-condition finding.

**Relevant context:** Boundary-condition extension of Artificial Hivemind diversity metrics. Pure sampling + embedding analysis on a single GPU.

# Cascading-failure simulation: how one shared model's blind spot propagates through a multi-agent pipeline

**Problem:** The International AI Safety Report 2026 flags cascading failures when critical systems depend on the same foundation model. There is no small, reproducible demonstration of how a single shared blind spot amplifies through a chained pipeline (generator -> checker -> summarizer all using the same backbone).

**Direction:** Build a toy 3-stage agent pipeline where stages share vs. differ in backbone model. Inject a known shared blind spot (a prompt all instances of model A mishandle). Measure end-to-end failure rate when all stages use A vs. when stages use distinct models. Quantify the cascade amplification from monoculture.

**Why it matters:** Turns the abstract 'cascading failure' open problem into a concrete, reproducible micro-demonstration that deployers and policymakers can understand. Builds a small reusable harness for monoculture stress-testing — strategically valuable infrastructure at prototype scale.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on International AI Safety Report 2026 cascading-failure concern. Small agent harness + open models on a consumer GPU; no training.

# Does instruction-tuning on shared data erase diversity? A before/after homogeneity comparison

**Problem:** A surprising-result hypothesis: base (pretrained-only) models may be MORE diverse than their instruction-tuned versions, because alignment/SFT on overlapping instruction datasets pulls models toward the same response style. If so, the very process meant to make models helpful/safe creates the hivemind.

**Direction:** Pair several open base models with their official instruction-tuned counterparts. On fixed open-ended prompts, measure inter-model homogeneity within the base set vs. within the instruct set. Test whether instruction tuning increases cross-model similarity (homogenization-by-alignment).

**Why it matters:** If alignment is a homogenization force, there is a real tension between safety tuning and diversity — a deeper root-cause finding for the hivemind. No training needed; both base and instruct checkpoints are public.

**Relevant context:** Targets the Artificial Hivemind root-cause open problem ('what causes output convergence'). Uses public base+instruct open checkpoints on a consumer GPU.

# Correlated value blind spots: do models share the same omissions in moral/ethical reasoning?

**Problem:** Homogeneity of *values* is a fuzzy-reward, hard-to-measure failure mode that labs under-invest in. If diverse models systematically omit the same considerations when reasoning about ethical dilemmas (same neglected stakeholders, same ignored harms), our AI ecosystem has a shared moral blind spot.

**Direction:** Use a set of ethical-dilemma / value-tradeoff prompts. For each, query 6-8 models and have an external rubric enumerate which canonical considerations each response raises vs. omits. Measure whether omissions are correlated across models (same considerations consistently missing) more than chance.

**Why it matters:** Shared value omissions mean swapping vendors doesn't fix a moral blind spot — a diffuse, long-horizon risk frontier labs deprioritize. Evaluating fuzzy-reward homogeneity needs no lab resources and is high counterfactual value.
